findings.title: Unauthenticated-style privilege escalation via query param plus misleading comments
findings.body: `use_optimized`/`enable_advanced` gates the OptimizedCursorPaginator on `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, triggered purely by a client-supplied query param `optimized_pagination=true`. Combined with OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset handling, this allows a privileged (but not necessarily organization-owner) user with global access to request negative offsets, bypassing normal pagination boundary protections. The comments ("Enable advanced pagination features for authorized administrators") assert safety without any actual validation that negative offsets can't be abused to view out-of-range/deleted data. This needs a security review and either removal or stronger justification/tests.

findings.title: Negative offset slicing can produce incorrect/duplicate results or wrap around
findings.body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset. Django querysets do not support negative indexing the way Python lists do (negative slice indices on QuerySet raise ValueError or behave unexpectedly depending on Django version), so this will either throw at runtime or silently return wrong results. There's no test covering this path (test files for buffer/spans don't test this paginator at all), so this bug is not caught in CI.

findings.title: Clamping offset to 0 silently changes paging semantics for BasePaginator
findings.body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters behavior from the previous unconditional `offset`. If `offset` was ever meant to be used as negative in some legitimate codepath (e.g. computed from cursor math elsewhere), clamping silently to 0 changes results without raising an error, making debugging harder. This introduces an undocumented behavior change to the widely-used BasePaginator affecting all paginator consumers (DateTimePaginator, Paginator), not just the new optimized one, with no accompanying tests validating offset-clamping behavior under normal and edge/negative-offset cursor values.

findings.title: Reduced redirect-depth traversal limit from 10000 to 1000 silently breaks deep segment merging
findings.body: The loop limit for following redirect chains was reduced from 10000 to 1000 with no comment explaining why, dropping the original comment noting "segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly." This means segment trees deeper than 1000 spans will now have redirects silently truncated/broken at a much lower threshold than before, a regression for very deep traces, without any test coverage for this specific boundary case.

findings.title: zpopmin eviction count can exceed available members and doesn't account for merges correctly
findings.body: After zunionstore calls, `span_count` is set to the returned cardinality of the unioned set, but if both branches (span_key and parent_key unions) execute, `span_count` is overwritten by the second zunionstore's result rather than reflecting the final cumulative count correctly if logic changes; also when `span_count` is 0 initially (both unions skipped) it falls back to `zcard` which is correct, but if only one union happens and leaves stale state, eviction via `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)` could evict legitimate spans that were just added before the current span is even added to `set_key`, since this script runs per-span before the current span's own zadd into `set_key` occurs. This can cause newly-ingested spans belonging to the same segment but processed in a later pipeline step to be evicted or the oldest-timestamp spans (by zscore, i.e. end_timestamp_precise) to be dropped even though the real intent is likely to cap by count irrespective of order, which may silently drop arbitrary spans from large segments without a corresponding test added for span-buffer.lua's eviction logic.
